course.title: Messaging and Events
course.description: The moment a system has two services, it has messages: "order placed", "payment failed", "send the reminder in an hour". Messaging is how services stay decoupled (the sender doesn't know who listens), absorb bursts (a queue soaks up a spike) and survive each other's outages (the message waits). It is also where most production incidents in distributed systems come from: duplicates, lost events, poison messages, retry storms and half-finished workflows. This module builds the patterns that keep all of that under control, small enough to hold in your head and exact enough to test.

lessons.title: Messaging and Events
lessons.explanation:
# 12 · Messaging and Events

The moment a system has two services, it has messages: "order placed",
"payment failed", "send the reminder in an hour". Messaging is how
services stay decoupled (the sender doesn't know who listens), absorb
bursts (a queue soaks up a spike) and survive each other's outages (the
message waits). It is also where most production incidents in
distributed systems come from: duplicates, lost events, poison
messages, retry storms and half-finished workflows. This module builds
the patterns that keep all of that under control, small enough to hold
in your head and exact enough to test.

## The mental model

### 1 · Delivery guarantees are a choice between duplicates and loss

A network can't tell "the consumer crashed before acking" from "the
ack got lost". So every broker picks one side:

| guarantee | what can go wrong | how it's built | you add |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| at-most-once | messages lost | ack before processing | nothing (accept loss) |
| at-least-once | messages duplicated | ack after processing; redeliver on doubt | an **idempotent consumer** |
| "exactly-once" | nothing, *inside one system* | at-least-once + dedupe, or a transaction spanning offset and effect | dedupe or transactions |

SQS standard queues, Google Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ with manual acks and a
Kafka consumer that commits offsets after processing are all
at-least-once.
"Exactly-once" in practice means exactly-once **effect**:

```java
if (seen.contains(msg.id())) return "duplicate";   // 1 check
effect.accept(msg);                                // 2 do it (may throw)
seen.add(msg.id());                                // 3 only now remember
```

### 2 · Queues need a limit and a policy

A queue between a fast producer and a slow consumer either grows
without bound (the outage just arrives later, as an OOM) or makes a
decision when full:

```
                 ┌─────────── capacity ───────────┐
producer ──▶ offer │ m1 │ m2 │ m3 │ m4 │ m5 │ m6 │ poll ──▶ consumer
                 └────────────────────────────────┘
full?  REJECT       → producer told "not now" (backpressure, nothing lost)
       DROP_OLDEST  → head discarded (freshest data wins: telemetry, prices)
       DROP_NEWEST  → new message discarded (protect accepted work)
```

Failures need a policy too: a message that fails goes to the **back**
of the queue (so it can't block the others), and after N attempts to a
**dead-letter queue** for a human to inspect and redrive.

### 3 · Never dual-write: the outbox

"Save the order, then publish OrderPlaced" loses the event if the
process dies in between; "publish, then save" announces orders that
don't exist. The fix is to make it one write:

```
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO orders  (id, cents)          VALUES ('o1', 500);
  INSERT INTO outbox  (seq, event, sent)   VALUES (41, 'OrderPlaced o1 500', false);
COMMIT
                         relay: SELECT ... WHERE NOT sent ORDER BY seq
                                publish(event); then UPDATE outbox SET sent = true
```

Publish-then-mark makes the relay at-least-once, which the consumers'
dedupe absorbs. Mark-then-publish is at-most-once, the bug you started
with.

### 4 · Events as the source of truth

Event sourcing stores the facts (`Opened`, `Deposited`, `Withdrawn`) and
derives state by folding them. Writes use **optimistic concurrency**:
"append these events if the stream is still at version 3". Reads use
**projections**: separate state built by replaying the log, which can
be dropped and rebuilt any time.

```java
Account state = null;
for (var e : events) state = apply(state, e);       // replay
store.append(id, state.version(), List.of(new Withdrawn(200)));  // or conflict
```

### 5 · Long workflows: sagas, not distributed transactions

A trip booking touches flights, hotels and cars, each with its own
database. A saga runs each local step, and on failure runs the
**compensations** of the steps that succeeded, newest first:

```
do flight ✓ → do hotel ✓ → do car ✗ "sold out"
                          undo hotel ✓ → undo flight ✓      = COMPENSATED
```

Compensations can fail, so they're retried (and must be idempotent);
when retries run out, the saga is **STUCK** and says so.

## The details that bite

1. **Remember a message id only after the effect succeeded.**
   Remembering first turns a crash into a message silently skipped on
   redelivery (exercise 03).
2. **A dedupe window must outlast the redelivery horizon.** An id that
   has aged out is applied again; size the window from the broker's
   redelivery behaviour, not from memory you'd like to save.
3. **Unsubscribe by subscription, not by handler.** The same handler
   can be subscribed twice; removing "the first equal handler" removes
   the wrong one (exercise 01).
4. **Isolate subscribers.** One throwing handler must not stop delivery
   to the rest; count the failure, keep going.
5. **Off by one on attempts.** With `maxAttempts = 3` the handler runs
   three times; the third failure dead-letters. Count attempts per
   queued *entry*, not per message text (exercise 04).
6. **Keep the last error, reset the count on redrive.** The last error
   is the one that gave up; a redriven message with an old count dies
   on the first blip.
7. **Stop the relay at the first failed publish.** Skipping ahead lets
   `OrderShipped` overtake `OrderPlaced` downstream (exercise 05).
8. **Fixed rate, not fixed delay, and no catch-up burst.** `next =
   runAt + period` keeps a timer anchored; then skip slots already in
   the past so a late timer runs once, not ten times (exercise 06).
9. **Optimistic concurrency needs the version you READ.** Appending
   with "whatever the version is now" defeats the check; two
   withdrawals of the last 100 both succeed (exercise 07).
10. **Don't compensate the step that failed, and don't stop unwinding
    when one compensation gives up** (exercise 08).

## Cheat table

| problem | pattern | real-world names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tell many services something happened | pub/sub topic | SNS, Kafka topics, RabbitMQ topic exchanges, Redis PUBLISH |
| producer faster than consumer | bounded queue + overflow policy | BlockingQueue, Reactor `onBackpressure*`, Akka `OverflowStrategy` |
| broker delivers twice | idempotent consumer / inbox table | message-id dedupe, a transactional inbox table |
| a message always fails | retry to the back, then DLQ | SQS `maxReceiveCount` + redrive, RabbitMQ DLX |
| DB write + publish must agree | transactional outbox + relay | Debezium CDC, polling publisher |
| "do this later" | delay queue / scheduler | SQS `DelaySeconds`, Sidekiq scheduled set, `ScheduledExecutorService` |
| audit trail, rebuildable read models | event sourcing + projections | EventStoreDB, Axon, ledgers |
| multi-service workflow | saga with compensations | Temporal, AWS Step Functions |

## How this connects

- **10-rate-limits-and-resilience**: retries with backoff and jitter,
  circuit breakers and idempotency keys are the producer side of the
  same problems; a DLQ is what's left when retries run out.
- **11-partitioning-and-ids**: Kafka orders messages per partition and
  picks the partition by hashing the key, so "all events for order 17
  in order" is a partitioning decision. Snowflake ids make good message
  ids for dedupe.
- **13-storage-and-consistency**: the outbox leans on a local
  transaction, event sourcing is a write-ahead log you keep forever,
  and a saga is the alternative to the two-phase commit coordinator
  built there.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-pubsub-bus.java` | ★☆☆ | topics, wildcards, isolated subscribers, unsubscribe |
| 02 | `02-bounded-queue.java` | ★☆☆ | backpressure with REJECT / DROP_OLDEST / DROP_NEWEST |
| 03 | `03-dedupe-consumer.java` | ★★☆ | an idempotent consumer with a bounded dedupe window |
| 04 | `04-dead-letter-queue.java` | ★★☆ | retries to the back, dead letters, redrive |
| 05 | `05-transactional-outbox.java` | ★★☆ | orders + outbox in one unit, an ordered relay |
| 06 | `06-delay-scheduler.java` | ★★☆ | delayed and recurring jobs with priorities and a fake clock |
| 07 | `07-event-sourcing.java` | ★★★ | replay, optimistic appends, commands, a projection |
| 08 | `08-saga-compensation.java` | ★★★ | a saga that unwinds, retries undos, and admits STUCK |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/13-storage-and-consistency`

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/01-.instructions:
**Concepts:** publish/subscribe · topics · wildcards · failure isolation  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Services announce facts ("orders.created") without knowing who listens.
Finish the nested class EventBus and its Subscription.matches.
subscribe(pattern, handler) returns a Runnable that unsubscribes
exactly that subscription (running it again does nothing). A pattern
is an exact topic, or ends in ".*" and matches every topic that starts
with the part before the "*" (prefix plus dot):
"orders.*" matches "orders.created" and "orders.eu.created", but not
"orders" or "ordersx.created". publish(topic, message) calls every
matching handler in subscription order and returns how many completed
normally. A handler that throws is skipped, counted by failures(), and
does not stop the rest. Subscribing the same handler twice delivers
twice.

    subscribe("orders.*", log::add)
    publish("orders.created", "#17")   → 1
    publish("payments.failed", "#17")  → 0

hint: keep one object per subscription; unsubscribe removes that one.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/01-.explanation:
Pub/sub decouples the code that notices something from the code that
reacts to it: the order service publishes "orders.created" and never
learns that billing, email and analytics subscribe. Guava's EventBus,
Spring application events, Redis PUBLISH/PSUBSCRIBE and RabbitMQ topic
exchanges are all this shape; Kafka and SNS are the same idea across
processes. Wildcard rules differ: in RabbitMQ "orders.*" matches exactly
one more word and "orders.#" any number, so this bus's ".*" behaves
like RabbitMQ's ".#" (minus the zero-word case).
Three details make a bus trustworthy. First, ordering: a List of
subscriptions gives deterministic delivery order. Second, isolation:
one buggy subscriber must not stop the others, so each call gets its
own try/catch, and the failure is counted (in production: logged and
metered) rather than swallowed silently. Third, unsubscribe must
remove exactly the subscription it came from. Removing "the first
entry whose handler equals this one" goes wrong when one handler is
subscribed twice; holding the Subscription object in the returned
Runnable and removing by identity cannot.
The wildcard check is startsWith(prefix + "."): without the dot,
"orders.*" would also match "ordersx.created", and "orders" alone is
not an event about an order. Iterate over a copy of the list so a
handler that unsubscribes during publish cannot break the loop.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/02-.instructions:
**Concepts:** backpressure · overflow policies · ArrayDeque · load shedding  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A producer can always outrun a consumer, so a real buffer has a limit
and a policy for when it is full. Finish the nested class
BoundedQueue(capacity, policy) (capacity < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException). offer(msg) returns whether msg is now in the
queue. When the queue is full: REJECT refuses msg (false, counted by
rejected(): the producer still holds it and must slow down);
DROP_OLDEST throws away the head and accepts msg (true); DROP_NEWEST
throws msg away (false). Thrown-away messages are counted by dropped().
poll() takes the head (Optional.empty() when empty). pollBatch(max)
takes up to max messages in FIFO order (max < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException). highWater() is the largest size reached.

    capacity 2, DROP_OLDEST:  offer(a) offer(b) offer(c)  → queue [b, c]
    capacity 2, REJECT:       offer(c)                   → false
    pollBatch(5) on [b, c]                               → [b, c]

hint: ArrayDeque gives you both ends; the policy only matters when full.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/02-.explanation:
An unbounded queue does not remove overload, it postpones it until the
heap runs out, and meanwhile every message waits longer. A bounded
queue forces the choice that exists anyway: when full, who loses?
REJECT is backpressure proper: the producer is told "not now" and keeps
the message, so nothing is lost but the producer must slow down or
buffer upstream (TCP windows, a full BlockingQueue, HTTP 429/503).
DROP_OLDEST keeps the freshest data and suits telemetry and live
prices, where a newer reading supersedes an old one. DROP_NEWEST
protects work already accepted and suits best-effort streams such as
debug logs. Akka Streams, Reactor's onBackpressureDrop/Latest and
Kafka producers' buffer.memory are this same menu.
Counting matters as much as the policy: rejected() and dropped() are
the metrics that tell an operator the system is shedding load, and
they are different things (a rejected message still exists; a dropped
one is gone). highWater() is the classic queue-depth gauge; a
high-water mark that sits at capacity means the consumer is too slow.
The usual bug is ordering: under DROP_OLDEST, pollFirst() the head
BEFORE offerLast(msg), or the queue briefly holds capacity + 1 and the
high-water mark lies.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/03-.instructions:
**Concepts:** at-least-once delivery · idempotent consumers · dedupe windows  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Brokers like SQS and Kafka deliver AT LEAST once, so a consumer sees
repeats. Finish the nested class DedupingConsumer(window, effect)
(window < 1 → IllegalArgumentException). handle(msg) runs
effect.accept(msg) and returns "applied <id>" the first time an id is
seen, or returns "duplicate <id>" without running the effect if the id
is remembered. If the effect throws, the exception propagates and the
id is NOT remembered, so a redelivery tries again. Only the last
`window` applied ids are remembered: when a new id would exceed it, the
oldest-applied id is forgotten (a duplicate does not refresh an id's
place). remembered() lists the remembered ids, oldest first.

    window 2:  handle(m1) → "applied m1"   handle(m1) → "duplicate m1"
               handle(m2), handle(m3)       remembered() → [m2, m3]
               handle(m1) → "applied m1"   (forgotten, so applied again)

hint: a LinkedHashSet remembers insertion order and answers contains.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/03-.explanation:
Exactly-once delivery across a network is not on offer: the broker
cannot tell "the consumer crashed before acking" from "the ack got
lost", so it redelivers. What you can build is exactly-once EFFECT:
at-least-once delivery plus a consumer that recognises repeats by
message id (the "idempotent consumer" / inbox pattern).
Order inside handle is the whole design. Check the id; run the effect;
only then remember the id. Remembering first turns a crash or a thrown
exception into a message that is silently never processed: the
redelivery arrives, looks like a duplicate, and is skipped. With the
effect first, the worst case is a duplicate effect after a crash, which
is the case the dedupe exists for. (In a real service, the effect and
the "seen" row go into one database transaction, which closes even
that gap; module 08's payments made the same choice.)
Memory is not free, so the seen-set is a window. A LinkedHashSet keeps
first-insertion order, so the eldest id is iterator().next(). The
window must be wider than the broker's redelivery horizon (SQS's
visibility timeout, a Kafka consumer's rewind after a rebalance):
anything older than the window is applied again, as one of the tests
shows. A duplicate does not re-add the id, so it keeps its original
place in line and ages out on schedule.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/04-.instructions:
**Concepts:** retries · poison messages · dead-letter queues · redrive  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

One malformed message must not wedge a queue forever. Finish the nested
class RetryQueue(maxAttempts) (maxAttempts < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException). submit(msg) appends to the queue.
processNext(handler) takes the head (empty queue →
NoSuchElementException) and calls handler.accept(msg). Success returns
"ok <msg>". A throw counts one attempt: below maxAttempts the message
goes to the BACK of the queue and the result is "retry <msg> (attempt
N)"; at maxAttempts it moves to the dead-letter list as Dead(msg,
attempts, the exception's message) and the result is "dead <msg> after
N attempts". drain(handler) calls processNext until the queue is empty
and returns the results in order. deadLetters() is read-only.
redrive() moves every dead letter, in order, back to the end of the
queue with a fresh attempt count, empties the list, and returns how
many moved. pending() is the queue length.

    maxAttempts 2, handler fails on "p":   submit(p) submit(x)
    drain(h) → [retry p (attempt 1), ok x, dead p after 2 attempts]

hint: a retry re-queues a NEW Entry carrying attempts + 1.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/04-.explanation:
A "poison message" is one that fails every time: bad JSON, a reference
to a deleted row, a bug that only that payload triggers. Retried in
place at the head of the queue, it blocks everything behind it
forever. Two rules fix that, and SQS, RabbitMQ and every job framework
(Sidekiq, Celery, Hangfire) implement both: a failed message goes to
the BACK of the queue so others get their turn, and after maxAttempts
it moves to a dead-letter queue where a human (or an alert) looks at
it. SQS calls the limit maxReceiveCount.
The attempt count belongs to the queued ENTRY, not to the message
text and not to the queue: a small Entry(msg, attempts) record is
enough. Counting attempts in a Map<String, Integer> keyed by the text
breaks the moment the same text is submitted twice.
Off-by-one is the classic bug: with maxAttempts = 3 the handler runs
three times and the third failure dead-letters (attempts == max), not
the fourth. maxAttempts = 1 means "no retries at all".
Keep the LAST error in the dead letter: the first error may have been
a transient timeout, while the last is what finally gave up.
redrive is the operator's tool after a fix is deployed: replay the
dead letters with fresh counters. Without resetting the count, a
redriven message that hits one more blip goes straight back to the
dead letters.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/05-.instructions:
**Concepts:** dual writes · outbox pattern · relays · at-least-once publishing  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Saving an order and publishing "OrderPlaced" are two writes, and either
can fail alone. Finish the nested class OrderService. placeOrder(id,
cents) stores the order AND appends the event "OrderPlaced <id>
<cents>" to its outbox, as one unit: a known id or cents < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException and neither is written. relay(publisher,
batchSize) sends the oldest unpublished events, at most batchSize, in
order, through publisher.accept(event), marking each published only
after accept returns. If accept throws, relay stops right there (the
event stays unpublished, the exception does not escape) and returns
how many it published this call. batchSize < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException. pending() lists unpublished events, oldest
first. purgePublished() deletes published rows and returns how many.

    placeOrder("o1", 500)   pending() → ["OrderPlaced o1 500"]
    relay(broker::send, 10) → 1        pending() → []
    a broker that is down:  relay(...) → 0, the event stays pending

hint: a Row holds an event and a published flag; never remove on send.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/05-.explanation:
The dual-write problem: "save to the database, then publish to the
broker" loses the event when the process dies between the two, and
"publish, then save" announces orders that never existed. No ordering
of two independent writes is safe. The transactional outbox makes it
one write: the event is a row in the SAME database transaction as the
order, so both exist or neither does. A separate relay (a poller, or
change-data-capture such as Debezium) reads the outbox and publishes.
The relay's rule is publish first, mark second. If it crashes between
the two, the event is sent again on restart: at-least-once, which the
consumers' dedupe (exercise 03) absorbs. Marking first would be
at-most-once: a crash after marking loses the event forever, which is
the bug the outbox exists to remove.
Stopping at the first failure keeps events in order. Skipping a failed
event and sending the next would let "OrderShipped" overtake
"OrderPlaced" downstream. The next relay starts again from the oldest
pending row, so the failed one is retried first.
Validation happens before either write, which is what "one unit"
means here; in SQL it is BEGIN ... COMMIT around both INSERTs.
purgePublished is the housekeeping job: outbox tables grow forever
unless published rows are deleted, but only published ones.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/06-.instructions:
**Concepts:** delayed jobs · priorities · fixed-rate timers · injected clocks  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Delayed jobs ("retry in 30 s", "send the reminder tomorrow") need a
scheduler. Finish the nested class Scheduler(clock), clock giving ms.
schedule(name, priority, delayMs) runs name once at now + delayMs.
every(name, priority, periodMs) runs at now + period, then again each
period at FIXED RATE: the next run is the previous run time + period,
skipping any slot that is already <= now when it runs (so a late timer
runs once, not in a burst). runDue() reads the clock once and runs
every task whose time is <= now, in order: higher priority first, then
earlier run time, then the order the tasks were first scheduled; it
returns their names. cancel(name) removes a pending task (false if
there is none). nextRunAt() is the earliest pending run time. Negative
delay, period < 1, or a name already pending →
IllegalArgumentException.

    now 0: schedule("a", 1, 50), every("tick", 0, 100)
    now 100: runDue() → [a, tick]     nextRunAt() → 200
    now 450: runDue() → [tick]        nextRunAt() → 500  (not 300, 550)

hint: next = runAt + period; while next <= now, add another period.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/06-.explanation:
Every queue that offers delayed delivery (SQS DelaySeconds, RabbitMQ's
delayed-message plugin, Sidekiq's scheduled set, a ScheduledExecutor)
is this: a set of (runAt, task) entries and a loop that runs what is
due. Two orderings matter. Among due tasks, priority decides; ties go
to the earlier run time, then to FIFO by scheduling order, so the
result is deterministic. A single PriorityQueue ordered by priority
alone would run a high-priority task before its time, so first filter
by runAt <= now, then sort the due ones.
Reading the clock ONCE per runDue gives the batch a consistent "now".
The recurring task is where the bugs live. Fixed DELAY (next = now +
period) drifts later every time a run is late. Fixed RATE (next =
runAt + period) keeps the schedule anchored, but if the process was
paused for many periods, a naive loop fires every missed slot at once:
a thundering burst. Skipping slots that are already <= now gives "run
once, then get back on schedule", which is how cron-like schedulers and
java.util.Timer users usually want it. Note the task keeps its first
scheduling order for tie-breaks, so a timer does not lose its place.
cancel and the "already pending" check both look the name up, so a
Map from name to entry keeps them O(1); the clock is a LongSupplier so
the tests can move time.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/07-.instructions:
**Concepts:** event sourcing · replay · optimistic concurrency · projections  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Store what HAPPENED, derive what IS. Events are Opened(owner),
Deposited(cents) and Withdrawn(cents). replay(events) folds a stream
into Account(owner, balance, version), version = events applied; an
empty stream, or one whose first event is not Opened (or that opens
twice) → IllegalStateException. EventStore.append(stream, expected,
events) adds events only if the stream currently has exactly
`expected` events, else IllegalStateException and nothing is added; it
returns the new length and also records each event in a global log as
Recorded(stream, version, event), version counting from 1.
events(stream) is a read-only list (empty when unknown). The commands
open, deposit and withdraw replay the stream, validate, and append ONE
event with the version they read: open needs an empty stream; deposit
and withdraw need an open account (else IllegalStateException), cents
>= 1 (else IllegalArgumentException), and withdraw needs enough money
(else IllegalStateException). balanceByOwner(log) projects the global
log into owner → total balance across that owner's accounts.

    open(s, "a1", "ada"); deposit(s, "a1", 500); withdraw(s, "a1", 200)
    replay(s.events("a1"))    → Account[owner=ada, balance=300, version=3]
    s.append("a1", 2, ...)    → IllegalStateException (stream is at 3)

hint: replay with one instanceof per event; a command only ever appends.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/07-.explanation:
In an event-sourced system the append-only list of events IS the
database; the current balance is a fold over it. You get an audit log
for free, can rebuild any past state (replay a prefix), and can build
new read models later by replaying history into them. Banks' ledgers,
EventStoreDB, Axon and Kafka-as-a-log architectures work this way.
replay is a left fold with a null "no account yet" state. Validating
the stream shape (Opened first, exactly once) catches corrupt or
mis-routed streams early instead of producing a balance for nobody.
Commands follow one rhythm: load (replay), decide (validate against
the replayed state), append with expectedVersion = the version you
loaded. That last argument is optimistic concurrency: if another
writer appended in between, the stream length no longer matches and
the append fails instead of silently interleaving. Two withdrawals of
the last 100 can then never both succeed; the loser reloads and is
refused. A command must append nothing when validation fails, so
validate everything before touching the store.
The projection reads the GLOBAL log, in append order, and keeps its own
state (stream → owner, owner → total). It never peeks at accounts, so
it could live in another process fed by a subscription (exercise 01)
and be thrown away and rebuilt at any time. Java 17 has no pattern
switch, so dispatch with instanceof patterns, one branch per event.

javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/08-.instructions:
**Concepts:** sagas · compensating actions · partial failure · retries  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Booking a trip touches three services and none of them share a
transaction. Write run(steps, compensationAttempts) (attempts < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException). It runs each Step's action in order,
logging "do <name>" after each success. When an action throws, it logs
"fail <name>: <message>", runs no later steps, and undoes the steps
that SUCCEEDED, newest first (the failed step is not undone). Each
compensation is tried up to compensationAttempts times: every failed
try logs "undo <name> failed: <message>", a success logs "undo
<name>". A compensation that never succeeds is given up on, and the
remaining compensations still run. The Result is COMPLETED (nothing
failed), COMPENSATED (a step failed and every undo succeeded) or STUCK
(some undo was given up on), plus the log.

    steps flight, hotel, car; car's action throws "sold out"
    → COMPENSATED, [do flight, do hotel, fail car: sold out,
                    undo hotel, undo flight]

hint: push each succeeded step on a stack; unwind it on failure.
javabootcamp/12-messaging-and-events/08-.explanation:
A saga replaces one distributed transaction (which needs every service
to hold locks and agree, as in two-phase commit, module 13) with a
sequence of LOCAL transactions, each paired with a compensating action
that semantically undoes it: cancel the flight, release the hotel
room. If step k fails, run the compensations of steps k-1 down to 1.
Uber's Cadence/Temporal, AWS Step Functions and Axon all orchestrate
sagas this way.
Reverse order matters because later steps may depend on earlier ones
(refund the charge before releasing the reservation it paid for). The
failed step is NOT compensated: it did not happen, or it rolled itself
back locally, and "undoing" it could cancel something it never did.
A stack (ArrayDeque push/pop) of succeeded steps captures both rules.
Compensations fail too: the hotel API times out like any other. So
they are retried, which means they must be idempotent: releasing a
room twice must be harmless. When retries run out the saga is STUCK:
the system is inconsistent and a human must step in, so the status
says so loudly instead of pretending to be COMPENSATED. Even then, the
other compensations still run; giving up on one is no reason to leave
the flight booked as well.
Sagas give up isolation: between "do hotel" and "undo hotel" other
users can see the booked room. That trade is the price of no locks.
